One of my favorite details of Sonner:

The toast can be swiped down to dismiss. Instead of prreventing the toast to be dragged upwards, you experience friction.

You can still drag it, but it will slow down and eventually stop. It’s nicer than just stopping the toast immediately.

An important skill in the AI era, next to knowing what to build, is knowing what to consume.  

AI tools are so powerful that you can absorb ideas and insights from more people than ever before.  

Knowing who is worth listening to is a very valuable skill these days.

Added a new /animation-performance skill to my skills repo.

It includes lots of rules that agents seem to skip at the moment.

Think about keeping blur() values small, not animating shadows, not swapping CSS variables frequently, etc.

The bigger an animated element is, the slower it should move.

Notice how the hand on the right moves much slower than the cursors on the left. That’s because it feels heavier.

The same applies to distance. The more an element has to travel, the longer the animation should be.

I’m like 98% sure that you should set `text-wrap: pretty;` by default globally in your app.

It gives you nicer line breaks (avoids orphans),which is what you want most of the time. Then fix the edge cases where orphans are actually what you need like some headings (edge case!).

Interesting to see how the AI companies are trying to make their apps feel more human, less alien. 

Muse has this cute little animated guy smiling all the time, ready to help you with anything. It feels friendlier and more relatable than a blank, sterile screen with an input.

ChatGPT Computer Use shows a moving cursor as it’s working. It’s not technically required, but it makes the whole process less scary and easier to follow.

It’s like the early iPhone days when things used to immitate real world objects so that an unfamiliar technology felt more intuitive and relatable. 

In this case we imitate presence, trying to give the AI a more human feel.
Migrated Linear from Radix to Base UI, took just over a milion tokens.

One nice subtle benefit of using Base UI over Radix is that the animations are interruptible since Base uses CSS transitions instead of keyframes.

The workflow looks roughly like this:
- Start with /prototype to see a few different variants, tell it to use /animate for the right easing and timing.
- Pick the variant you like and iterate on it. This is just asking the agent to correct/change some details.
- Run a /prep-for-prod skill on it. This contains perf, a11y, and mobile checks.

Since almost every “taste” decision related to animation has a logical reason, this can get you pretty far even when you don’t know much about motion.

You can get pretty close to this workflow by using my public skills (thanks for 1.4 milion downloads!)

- Holding ⌘ shows each tab’s keyboard shortcut, like ⌘1, ⌘2, etc. (wish Chrome did that).
